extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students studying equitable remedies for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and legal standards governing applications for, and defenses to, injunctions in equity for patent infringement, and the evidence appropriate at different stages of a patent cause (title vs infringement). Covers notice, affidavits, defenses (acquiescence, public use, estoppel), and evidentiary burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reluctance to dissolve injunction for mere technical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Court should not dissolve an injunction for doubts on technical objections (e.g., clerical mistakes in letters-patent or signatures by acting officers) unless imperative principles of law show the letters-patent to be clearly void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If mischievous consequences are likely from interfering and legislative measures are pending to remedy possible public mistakes, the injunction already granted should not be dissolved for such technical objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of license/contract/use under permission on injunction relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Where defendant has used the invention under a license or contract, especially where rent/payments were made under a draft license and benefit received, the court will consider ordering money to be paid into court to await the result of an action at law rather than dissolving or granting injunctive relief outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant has had the benefit of works erected under contract and the patentee has kept contracts with the defendant (not interposed to deprive benefit of expenditure), equity may treat the situation differently; money may be paid into court or an undertaking required as terms for continuing or dissolving injunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel and failure of consideration defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant who can show a total failure of consideration for a contract may defend at law against claims for rent/compensation; estoppel (including estoppel by recital) may also bar or permit certain defenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between total failure of consideration (a ground for legal defense) and estoppel doctrines (e.g., estoppel by recital). The court will consider whether prior dealings estop the defendant from disputing the patentee's title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use, dedication, or acquiescence as bar to equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee, after obtaining his patent, dedicates or surrenders it to public use, or acquiesces for a long period in public use without objection, he is not entitled to equitable relief such as an injunction; such acquiescence may amount to a dedication or surrender to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ground for refusing relief is that the patentee's conduct may have led or encouraged defendants or the public to use the invention. A qualified or limited surrender should be publicly notified so persons may guard against losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence or encouragement of defendants' use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee has openly encouraged or silently acquiesced in use by the very defendants he later seeks to enjoin, equity will refuse to interfere, because such conduct may mislead and cause expense or surprise amounting to unfairness or fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine applies even where the legal right exists; equitable relief is withheld when plaintiff's own conduct produced the complained-of use or led defendants to expend in reliance upon it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of notice for injunction applications in U.S. equity courts
rubrics_metrics.description: In U.S. courts of equity, an injunction to restrain patent infringement cannot be applied for without notice to the adverse party; therefore the injunction is always special (i.e., applied for with notice and opportunity to oppose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an answer has been filed, the plaintiff must typically present affidavits and allow the defendant opportunity to oppose; special injunctions differ from ex parte or common injunction practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/evidence requirements when applying for injunction after answer
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking an injunction after the defendant has filed an answer, the plaintiff must read affidavits to show title and the fact of infringement; these affidavits should, in strictness, cover issuing of the patent, novelty of the invention, and other facts necessary to title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the bill sets out the whole title and is sworn to and the defendant does not deny by affidavit, it is sometimes considered verified by the bill and affidavits may not be necessary; but if the defendant attacks the title by affidavit, the plaintiff must support the title by auxiliary proof to make out a prima facie right to an injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit disagreement on admissibility of affidavits after answer
rubrics_metrics.description: There is judicial disagreement whether, after an answer denying title, the plaintiff may read affidavits to contradict the answer (McLean: not entitled; Woodbury: may do so). The better view permits the plaintiff to fortify his right to an injunction with counter-evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author inclines to the view that the plaintiff may read affidavits after answer to show the case differs from the defendant's answer; the court's discretion governs this practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's sound discretion in granting or dissolving injunctions in irreparable-mischief cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The granting and dissolving of injunctions in cases of irreparable mischief rests in the sound discretion of the court, both before and after answer; affidavits may be read by either side even if they contradict the answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court must look into the evidence sufficiently to determine whether it is probable the plaintiff will establish his patent and grant or withhold an injunction accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of evidence in patent causes: title vs infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence in a patent cause divides into (1) evidence of title (letters-patent, plaintiff's interest, novelty, utility, sufficiency of specification) and (2) evidence of infringement (identity of thing made/used/practised by defendant with the patentee's invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor proof and witnesses to which category is at issue at each stage of proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of letters-patent under Statute of 1836 and necessity to produce referenced prior patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy of the patent under the seal of the patent office and the commissioner's signature is competent evidence a patent has been granted; if the patent produced refers to the description in a former patent, that former patent must be produced to show what the invention is if it is not made clear by the current patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure documentary chain is complete: produce earlier patents when later patents incorporate or refer to them to make invention intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters-patent as prima facie evidence of first inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Once letters-patent are proved to have issued, they are prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first inventor; because the statute requires oath that he is the first and true inventor, the burden of proof shifts to the objector to show the grant was improperly obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law presumes regularity of public officers and the sufficiency of proofs presented to them; challengers must produce evidence to overcome this presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trade witnesses to prove novelty (negative proof by exhausting affirmative instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: To strengthen title and rebut assertions of prior invention, the patentee may call persons 'who were in the way of hearing of the invention' to testify that they have not heard of it; the plaintiff's proposition is strictly a negative and must be supported by exhausting affirmative instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more such witnesses who by trade or position would have known of the invention yet had not heard of it, the stronger the evidence of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of negative trade testimony and treatment of prior experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative testimony that persons in the trade had not heard of the invention carries significant weight; prior experiments by others that did not reach completion will not necessarily defeat a later inventor's valid patent — the jury must decide whether prior efforts rested in experiment alone or achieved completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior efforts were merely experimental, a subsequent inventor who achieved the perfected result may still obtain a valid patent. Testimony that the invention was not known among relevant trade persons before the patentee strengthens the presumption of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's own declarations as evidence of time of completion (res gestae)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rebut defendant evidence of earlier use, the patentee may give his own declarations, as part of the res gestae, describing the nature and objects of the invention to show the precise time when he completed the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of contemporaneous statements by the patentee can be important to establish date of completion when the timing of invention is in dispute.
